web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: From Near-Bankruptcy to Rack-Scale AI — How AMD Got Here
question: How did Advanced Micro Devices evolve from a 1969 Silicon Valley second-source chipmaker into a fabless data center compute powerhouse, and how did its revenue and margins behave across past semiconductor boom-bust cycles?

epigraph.quote: You cannot shrink your way to greatness in semiconductors; you have to bet the company on the right architecture five years before the market sees it.
epigraph.author: Semiconductor industry maxim

web_blocks.title: 1.1 Founding Roots (1969–2009): The Second-Source Survivor Goes Fabless

web_blocks.html: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD) started on May 1, 1969, in Sunnyvale, California [1]. Jerry Sanders and seven former Fairchild Semiconductor engineers founded the firm [1]. For three decades, AMD lived in Intel's shadow as a second-source x86 chip supplier. In 1982, IBM forced Intel to sign a cross-license with AMD to secure a backup PC vendor. That legal pact gave AMD its lasting right to design x86 chips. Yet owning chip factories nearly broke the firm.

In 2006, AMD paid $5.4 billion for graphics maker ATI Technologies. That deal added Radeon GPUs and seeded AMD's future in accelerated compute. Soon after, ATI's debt hit the 2008 financial crisis and rising factory costs. AMD could not match Intel's fab spending. In March 2009, AMD spun off its fabs into GlobalFoundries and turned fabless [1]. The move avoided bankruptcy, but rigid Wafer Supply Agreement minimums tied AMD to older nodes for years.

web_blocks.title: 1.2 The Near-Death Trough & Lisa Su's Chiplet Revolution (2014–2021)

web_blocks.html: By October 2014, when Dr. Lisa Su became President and Chief Executive Officer, AMD stood on the brink of distress. Its Bulldozer CPU architecture trailed Intel on performance and power efficiency, server CPU share had collapsed below 1%, and annual revenue fell to $4,319 million in FY2016 with a GAAP operating loss of $373 million and a net loss of $498 million [5]. Stockholders' equity stood at just $477 million against $1,435 million in long-term debt [5].

Su made two defining strategic bets that reshaped the semiconductor industry. First, she concentrated AMD's scarce R&D budget on a clean-sheet CPU core called Zen, led by chief architect Jim Keller and later Mike Clark. Second, rather than building giant monolithic silicon dies that suffered poor manufacturing yields, AMD pioneered a modular chiplet architecture stitched together by high-speed Infinity Fabric interconnects. By pairing small compute chiplets built on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's (TSMC) leading-edge nodes with mature I/O dies, AMD slashed manufacturing costs per core and scaled core counts faster than Intel.

The payoff was dramatic. Zen debuted in 2017 across Ryzen PC processors and EPYC server chips, returning AMD to GAAP operating profitability ($127 million on $5,253 million revenue) [5]. As Intel stumbled on its 10-nanometer manufacturing node between 2018 and 2021, AMD captured wave after wave of cloud server and desktop share. Revenue surged from $6,731 million in FY2019 to $16,434 million in FY2021, while GAAP operating income climbed nearly sixfold from $631 million to $3,648 million [5]. Free cash flow jumped from $276 million in FY2019 to $3,220 million in FY2021, allowing AMD to eliminate virtually all long-term debt [5].

web_blocks.title: 1.3 The Xilinx Diversification & The 2022–2023 Semiconductor Digestion Cycle

web_blocks.html: In February 2022, AMD closed its transformative $49 billion all-stock acquisition of Xilinx, the global leader in Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) and adaptive System-on-Chip (SoC) silicon [1]. The deal added high-margin embedded revenues across aerospace, defense, industrial, automotive, and communications, while also bringing $24.1 billion in acquisition-related intangibles and nearly $24 billion in goodwill onto AMD's balance sheet [5]. Later in 2022, AMD also acquired Pensando Systems for $1.9 billion to add programmable Data Processing Units (DPUs) for cloud networking.

During the 2023 slump, AMD kept R&D high and pushed hard into AI chips. Its Instinct MI300X GPU scaled past $5 billion in FY2024 sales. Total FY2024 revenue rose 13.7% to $25,785 million, while GAAP EBIT recovered to $1,900 million [1][5]. Next, AMD bought key pieces to close the systems gap with NVIDIA. It bought European AI lab Silo AI for $665 million cash in August 2024 [13]. In March 2025, it bought hyperscale rack designer ZT Systems for $4,409 million [2]. Seven months later, AMD sold ZT's low-margin factories to Sanmina for $2.4 billion headline cash plus stock and an earn-out [2][8].

web_blocks.title: 1.4 The AI Pivot, Rack-Scale Engineering & Mega-Deals (2024–2026)
web_blocks.html: In FY2025, revenue climbed 34.3% to $34,639 million [1]. AMD grew fast even after taking an ~$800 million Q2 2025 charge on China-bound MI308 chips [1][9]. Then came a major shift in scale and risk between late 2025 and November 2026. AMD signed twin 6-gigawatt Instinct MI450 deals with OpenAI (October 2025) and Meta (February 2026) [6][7]. To anchor both pacts, AMD granted each partner a penny warrant for up to 160 million shares [6][7]. In Q3 2026, initial Helios racks lifted Data Center sales 97% YoY to $8,546 million and total sales to $13,377 million [2][3]. Management guided Q4 2026 revenue to roughly $17.0 billion [3]. In November 2026, AMD also closed two big AI deals totaling ~$11.1 billion: World Labs (~$8.2 billion all-stock) and Taalas (~$2.9 billion cash and stock) [2][10][11][12].

Rather than cutting R&D during the 2023 trough, AMD accelerated its pivot into generative AI accelerators. The Instinct MI300X GPU ramped from zero to over $5 billion in FY2024 data center AI sales, lifting consolidated revenue 13.7% to $25,785 million and restoring GAAP operating income to $1,900 million [1][5]. To close the software and systems gap against NVIDIA, AMD executed an aggressive sequence of capability acquisitions: European AI lab Silo AI ($665 million cash, August 2024) for enterprise model optimization [13]; hyperscale server designer ZT Systems ($4,409 million total consideration, March 2025) to build full rack-scale AI systems, followed by the October 2025 divestiture of ZT's low-margin manufacturing arm to Sanmina ($2.4 billion headline cash plus stock and earn-out) to preserve AMD's capital-light model [2][8].

In FY2025, AMD hit $34,639 million in revenue (+34.3% YoY) despite absorbing an ~$800 million Q2 2025 inventory and reserve charge after U.S. export controls restricted MI308 shipments to China [1][9]. Then, between October 2025 and November 2026, AMD fundamentally altered its scale and risk profile. It signed twin 6-gigawatt Instinct MI450 GPU partnerships with OpenAI (October 2025) and Meta Platforms (February 2026), issuing each partner a performance-based warrant for up to 160 million shares at $0.01 per share [6][7]. In Q3 2026, initial Helios rack-scale and MI450 shipments drove Data Center revenue up 97% YoY to $8,546 million and total revenue to a record $13,377 million (+45% YoY), with Q4 2026 revenue guided to roughly $17.0 billion [2][3]. Finally, in November 2026, AMD closed two frontier AI acquisitions totaling ~$11.1 billion: Fei-Fei Li's spatial-intelligence lab World Labs (~$8.2 billion all-stock) and specialized inference-chip startup Taalas (~$2.9 billion cash and stock) [2][10][11][12].

web_blocks.takeaway: AMD has survived multiple existential hardware cycles by shedding physical fabs in 2009, betting on modular TSMC chiplets in 2017, and now pivoting from standalone silicon chips to full rack-scale AI infrastructure.

web_blocks.html: This 57-year arc highlights two enduring traits of AMD. First, management repeatedly survived crises by making bold architectural pivots—going fabless in 2009, betting on chiplets in 2017, and moving to rack-scale AI in 2025 [1][2]. Second, every boom has carried sharp profit cyclicality when end-market inventories reset, as shown in FY2023 [1][5].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Advanced Micro Devices, you and I have to start with a survival story that almost ended in bankruptcy ten years ago. Founded in 1969 by Jerry Sanders and seven engineers who walked out of Fairchild Semiconductor, AMD spent most of its first four decades as the scrappy underdog living under Intel's shadow. A 1982 cross-license agreement forced by IBM gave AMD the legal right to build x86 processors, yet owning semiconductor factories nearly crushed the business. In 2009, burdened by debt from buying graphics maker ATI, AMD spun off its fabs into GlobalFoundries and committed to a fabless future.

When Dr. Lisa Su took over as CEO in October 2014, AMD was hanging by a thread. Its server market share had vanished below one percent. By 2016, annual revenue sat at just 4.3 billion dollars, GAAP operating losses hit 373 million dollars, and stockholders' equity had withered to 477 million dollars against more than 1.4 billion dollars in debt. Most executives in that chair would have slashed research and managed a slow decline. Su did the exact opposite. She bet the entire company on a brand-new processor core called Zen and a radical packaging philosophy called chiplets.

Instead of printing one giant, fragile silicon slab where a single microscopic dust speck ruins the whole chip, AMD broke its processors into small, high-yielding compute tiles connected by an ultra-fast highway called Infinity Fabric. Pairing those tiles with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's leading-edge fabs allowed AMD to pack far more cores onto a server socket at a fraction of Intel's manufacturing cost. Between 2017 and 2021, revenue more than tripled to 16.4 billion dollars, GAAP operating profit exploded to 3.65 billion dollars, and AMD wiped out its net debt.

book_subsections.title: The Xilinx Mega-Deal and the 2023 Cyclical Reality Check
paragraphs: Flush with momentum, AMD closed its 49-billion-dollar all-stock acquisition of Xilinx in February 2022, instantly becoming the global leader in programmable FPGAs and adaptive embedded silicon. Months later, it added Pensando Systems for data center networking. On paper, AMD looked diversified and bulletproof. In reality, semiconductor cycles rarely respect neat corporate strategy decks.

Almost immediately after Xilinx closed, post-pandemic PC demand cratered, gaming console volumes rolled over, and industrial buyers began burning off stockpiled FPGA chips. Consolidated revenue slipped from 23.6 billion dollars in 2022 to 22.7 billion dollars in 2023. Because AMD refused to slash R&D and had to absorb 2.8 billion dollars in annual non-cash amortization from Xilinx's acquired intangibles, GAAP operating profit plunged 89 percent from its 2021 peak down to just 401 million dollars. That painful downturn reminds us that even a fabless semiconductor winner remains deeply cyclical whenever multiple end markets digest inventory at once.

book_subsections.title: Why the Chiplet Bet Changed Semiconductor Economics Forever
paragraphs: To appreciate why AMD's turnaround was not mere luck, you and I have to understand the basic physics of silicon manufacturing. When a semiconductor foundry prints processors onto a circular 300-millimeter silicon wafer, microscopic defects scatter randomly across the glass. If you design one massive monolithic server chip—the way Intel built Xeon for decades—a single dust particle ruins the entire die. Your yield drops, and your cost per working processor explodes.

AMD's Zen engineers flipped that geometry on its head. Instead of printing one huge slab, they printed dozens of tiny, identical eight-core compute chiplets on TSMC's most advanced node, then paired them on a shared package with a larger input-output die built on cheaper, mature silicon. Smaller chiplets dramatically increased the percentage of defect-free chips harvested from every wafer. That single architectural insight let AMD pack 64, 96, 128, and now 256 cores into a server socket while keeping unit manufacturing costs far below Intel's monolithic rivals.

Even better, the exact same chiplet philosophy carried straight into AMD's Instinct AI accelerators. By stacking multiple compute dies alongside High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) stacks on TSMC's CoWoS packaging, AMD could scale memory capacity and bandwidth aggressively—first with MI300X in 2024, then MI355X in 2025, and now the MI450 Series inside Helios racks in late 2026. Yet every architectural revolution creates its own dependency: by shedding its factories in 2009 and embracing leading-edge chiplets, AMD traded internal fab capex for total reliance on TSMC's wafer and packaging capacity in Taiwan.

book_subsections.title: Reading AMD's Past Cycles Before Forecasting the Next One
paragraphs: Whenever a technology stock is growing revenue at 45 to 66 percent year-over-year, investors develop collective amnesia about cyclicality. Don't let that happen to you. Look back at AMD's own 2022 to 2023 history. Just months after closing the Xilinx deal, PC shipments fell off a cliff, gaming console demand cooled, and industrial buyers sat on two years of excess FPGA stock. Revenue barely dipped—down less than four percent—yet GAAP operating profit fell 89 percent from its 2021 high because R&D and acquisition amortization do not shrink when customers pause orders.

Today's AMD is far more weighted toward Data Center infrastructure than in 2022, which is a huge structural upgrade. Still, hyperscaler AI capital spending moves in waves too. Knowing how sharply AMD's fixed R&D and amortization amplify both upswings and downswings is the single best defense against mistaking a cyclical peak for a straight-line forever trend.

book_subsections.title: The 2024–2026 Transformation: From Chips to Gigawatt AI Systems
paragraphs: AMD used that 2023 trough to launch its second great reinvention: becoming the primary merchant challenger to NVIDIA in artificial intelligence accelerators. Its Instinct MI300X GPU crossed five billion dollars in 2024 sales, and in 2025 total revenue jumped 34 percent to 34.6 billion dollars—even after U.S. export rules forced an 800-million-dollar second-quarter inventory charge on China-bound MI308 chips.

Realizing that hyperscalers no longer buy bare GPUs—they buy liquid-cooled, rack-scale AI supercomputers—Lisa Su moved fast. AMD bought ZT Systems in March 2025 for 4.4 billion dollars to capture its rack-design engineering bench, then cleanly sold ZT's low-margin assembly factories to Sanmina seven months later. Then came the boldest commercial gambit in AMD's history. Between October 2025 and February 2026, AMD signed twin six-gigawatt Instinct MI450 GPU partnerships with OpenAI and Meta Platforms, sweetening each deal with a 160-million-share penny warrant tied to deployment milestones. By the third quarter of 2026, Helios racks were live at Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, pushing quarterly revenue to a record 13.4 billion dollars with fourth-quarter guidance near 17 billion dollars. And in November 2026, AMD closed two more bold bets—8.2 billion dollars in stock for Fei-Fei Li's spatial-intelligence lab World Labs and 2.9 billion dollars for inference-chip pioneer Taalas.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Pause and appreciate the two sides of AMD's evolution. On one hand, Lisa Su has executed one of the greatest operational turnarounds in corporate history—lifting revenue nearly eightfold from 4.3 billion dollars in 2016 to a 52-billion-dollar-plus run rate in 2026. On the other hand, winning the AI rack war has forced AMD to take on massive new commitments: 320 million customer warrant shares, 11.1 billion dollars in frontier AI acquisitions, and tens of billions in supply-chain obligations. The business is bigger and stronger than ever, yet its margin for error in the next cycle has narrowed.
